Histograms were used to examine the distribution of the chemical features in the Wine Quality dataset. These plots help identify the spread, concentration, and possible skewness of each variable.

Correlation Heatmap¶

A correlation heatmap was created to examine the relationships between the chemical features and wine quality. Correlation values range from -1 to +1. Values close to +1 indicate a strong positive relationship, while values close to -1 indicate a strong negative relationship. Values close to 0 indicate a weak or no linear relationship.

Class Imbalance¶

The distribution of wine quality scores was examined to determine whether all quality classes are equally represented. The results show that some quality scores have considerably more observations than others.

This indicates class imbalance in the dataset. In particular, the extreme quality scores tend to have fewer observations compared with the more common middle quality scores.

Class imbalance can affect machine learning models because the model may become biased towards the majority classes. As a result, the model may perform well on common quality scores but perform poorly when predicting underrepresented scores.

Therefore, accuracy alone may not be sufficient for evaluating the model. Metrics such as precision, recall, F1-score, and a confusion matrix should also be considered. Techniques such as class weighting, oversampling, or undersampling may also be considered if the imbalance significantly affects model performance.

Feature Engineering: Wine Quality Groups¶

The original quality variable contains several individual quality scores. To make the target variable easier to use for classification modelling, the scores were grouped into three categories:

  • Low: quality scores 3–4
  • Medium: quality scores 5–6
  • High: quality scores 7–8

A three-class approach was selected instead of a binary good/bad classification because it preserves more information from the original quality scores. It also allows the model to distinguish between low-, medium-, and high-quality wines.

This grouping can make the classification problem more practical and easier to interpret. However, the class distribution should be checked because the Low and High groups may contain fewer observations than the Medium group. If the imbalance is substantial, techniques such as class weighting or resampling may be considered during modelling.

Train/test split with stratification to preserve class ratios¶

# Import the required library
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Create the 3 quality groups
def quality_group(score):
    if score <= 4:
        return "Low"
    elif score <= 6:
        return "Medium"
    else:
        return "High"

df["quality_group"] = df["quality"].apply(quality_group)

# Select the chemical features
X = df[[
    "fixed acidity",
    "volatile acidity",
    "citric acid",
    "residual sugar",
    "chlorides",
    "free sulfur dioxide",
    "total sulfur dioxide",
    "density",
    "pH",
    "sulphates",
    "alcohol"
]]

# Select the target
y = df["quality_group"]

# Split the data into 80% training and 20% testing
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.20,
    random_state=42,
    stratify=y
)

# Display the results

print("Testing data:", X_test.shape)

print("\nTraining class distribution:")
print(y_train.value_counts())

print("\nTesting class distribution:")
print(y_test.value_counts())

Train/Test Split with Stratification¶

The dataset was divided into two parts: 80% training data and 20% testing data.

The quality_group variable was used as the target variable, with the wine quality scores grouped into three categories: Low, Medium, and High.

Stratified sampling was applied to ensure that the proportion of Low, Medium, and High quality wines remained approximately the same in both the training and testing datasets.

This approach is important because the Wine Quality dataset has an uneven distribution of quality classes. Maintaining similar class proportions helps the machine learning model learn from representative data and provides a more reliable evaluation of its performance.

A random_state of 42 was used to ensure that the same train/test split can be reproduced whenever the code is run.

Train 3 classifiers: Random Forest, Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), and Support Vector Classifier (SVC)¶

In [54]:
# ============================================
# WINE QUALITY - TRAIN 3 CLASSIFIERS
# ============================================

import pandas as pd

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC


# 2. CREATE QUALITY GROUPS
def create_quality_group(score):
    if score <= 4:
        return "Low"
    elif score <= 6:
        return "Medium"
    else:
        return "High"


df["quality_group"] = df["quality"].apply(create_quality_group)


# 3. SELECT FEATURES
features = [
    "fixed acidity",
    "volatile acidity",
    "citric acid",
    "residual sugar",
    "chlorides",
    "free sulfur dioxide",
    "total sulfur dioxide",
    "density",
    "pH",
    "sulphates",
    "alcohol"
]

X = df[features]
y = df["quality_group"]


# 4. SPLIT DATA
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.20,
    random_state=42,
    stratify=y
)


# 5. SCALE FEATURES FOR SGD AND SVC
scaler = StandardScaler()

X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)


# 6. RANDOM FOREST
random_forest = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=100,
    random_state=42
)

random_forest.fit(X_train, y_train)


# 7. SGD CLASSIFIER
sgd = SGDClassifier(
    max_iter=1000,
    random_state=42
)

sgd.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)


# 8. SUPPORT VECTOR CLASSIFIER
svc = SVC(
    random_state=42
)

svc.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)


# 9. MAKE PREDICTIONS
rf_pred = random_forest.predict(X_test)

sgd_pred = sgd.predict(X_test_scaled)

svc_pred = svc.predict(X_test_scaled)


# 10. CONFIRM EVERYTHING WORKED
print("Models trained successfully!")
print("--------------------------------")
print("Random Forest:        OK")
print("SGD Classifier:       OK")
print("Support Vector (SVC): OK")

print("\nTraining rows:", len(X_train))
print("Testing rows:", len(X_test))

Training Classification Models¶

Three machine learning classification models were trained to predict wine quality groups: Random Forest, Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), and Support Vector Classifier (SVC).

The wine quality scores were grouped into three categories: Low, Medium, and High. The dataset was divided into 80% training data and 20% testing data using stratified sampling to maintain the class proportions.

Standardisation was applied to the features used by SGD and SVC because these algorithms are sensitive to differences in feature scales. Random Forest was trained using the original feature values because scaling is not required for tree-based models.

The three models were trained using the same training data and will be compared using their performance on the test data.

Evaluate each: accuracy, classification report, confusion matrix¶

svc_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, svc_pred)

# Model names and accuracy values

# Add accuracy values on top of bars

    plt.text(
        bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2,
        value + 0.02,
        f"{value:.2%}",
        ha="center"
    )

plt.show()

Model Evaluation and Visualisation¶

The three classification models — Random Forest, Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), and Support Vector Classifier (SVC) — were evaluated using their predictions on the test dataset.

A bar chart was used to compare the accuracy of the three models. Accuracy represents the proportion of wine quality predictions that were correctly classified.

Confusion matrices were also created for each model to provide a more detailed view of the predictions. The matrices show the number of wines that were correctly and incorrectly classified as Low, Medium, or High quality.

The values along the diagonal of each confusion matrix represent correct predictions, while values outside the diagonal represent incorrect predictions.

These visualisations make it easier to compare the performance of the three classifiers and identify which quality classes are more difficult for each model to predict.

Random Forest Feature Importance¶

A feature importance chart was created to identify which chemical properties contribute most to predicting wine quality. The Random Forest model assigns an importance score to each feature based on its contribution to the model's predictions.

Higher importance scores indicate that a feature has a greater influence on the model's classification of wine quality, while lower scores indicate less influence. This helps identify the chemical properties that are most useful for predicting whether a wine is classified as Low, Medium, or High quality.

Comparison table: summarise the performance of all 3 models side-by-side¶

In [89]:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

# -----------------------------------
# 1. MAKE PREDICTIONS
# -----------------------------------

rf_pred = random_forest.predict(X_test)

sgd_pred = sgd.predict(X_test_scaled)

svc_pred = svc.predict(X_test_scaled)


# -----------------------------------
# 2. CALCULATE MODEL PERFORMANCE
# -----------------------------------

models = ["Random Forest", "SGD", "SVC"]

accuracy = [
    accuracy_score(y_test, rf_pred),
    accuracy_score(y_test, sgd_pred),
    accuracy_score(y_test, svc_pred)
]

precision = [
    precision_score(y_test, rf_pred, average="weighted", zero_division=0),
    precision_score(y_test, sgd_pred, average="weighted", zero_division=0),
    precision_score(y_test, svc_pred, average="weighted", zero_division=0)
]

recall = [
    recall_score(y_test, rf_pred, average="weighted", zero_division=0),
    recall_score(y_test, sgd_pred, average="weighted", zero_division=0),
    recall_score(y_test, svc_pred, average="weighted", zero_division=0)
]

f1 = [
    f1_score(y_test, rf_pred, average="weighted", zero_division=0),
    f1_score(y_test, sgd_pred, average="weighted", zero_division=0),
    f1_score(y_test, svc_pred, average="weighted", zero_division=0)
]


# -----------------------------------
# 3. CREATE COMPARISON TABLE
# -----------------------------------

comparison_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Model": models,
    "Accuracy": accuracy,
    "Precision": precision,
    "Recall": recall,
    "F1-Score": f1
})


# -----------------------------------
# 4. ROUND THE RESULTS
# -----------------------------------

comparison_table["Accuracy"] = comparison_table["Accuracy"].round(3)
comparison_table["Precision"] = comparison_table["Precision"].round(3)
comparison_table["Recall"] = comparison_table["Recall"].round(3)
comparison_table["F1-Score"] = comparison_table["F1-Score"].round(3)


# -----------------------------------
# 5. DISPLAY THE TABLE
# -----------------------------------

comparison_table

Comparison of Model Performance¶

The performance of the three classification models was compared using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score.

Random Forest, SGD, and SVC were evaluated using the same test dataset. This provides a fair comparison of their ability to classify wines into Low, Medium, and High quality groups.

The model with the strongest overall combination of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score will be considered the best-performing model. Since the dataset has class imbalance, F1-score, precision, and recall are considered alongside accuracy when selecting the final model.

Conclusion and Model Selection¶

The three classification models — Random Forest, SGD, and SVC — were compared using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score.

Based on the evaluation results, the [best-performing model] is the most suitable model for deployment because it achieved the strongest overall performance across the evaluation metrics.

The F1-score is particularly important because the Wine Quality dataset has an imbalanced class distribution. A model that performs well across precision and recall is more reliable than one that achieves high accuracy by mainly predicting the majority class.

Therefore, [ best-performing model] is recommended for deployment because it provides the best balance between correctly identifying the different wine quality groups and maintaining reliable predictions across the Low, Medium, and High classes.

Before deployment, the model should be further tested on new, unseen wine data to confirm that its performance remains consistent in a real-world environment.
